slides.title: Deadlock Avoidance
slides.body: Deadlock Avoidance

slides.title: Deadlock Avoidance
slides.body:
Why Prevention Falls Short?
Deadlock prevention denies a condition outright, even when no deadlock would occur
slides.notes: Alright, we've seen that prevention guarantees a deadlock-free system, but it's often too restrictive. It applies the same rules to every resource request, even in situations where no deadlock would actually occur. As a result, resource utilization, concurrency, and overall system throughput can suffer. Deadlock avoidance takes a different approach by making decisions dynamically, granting requests only when it's safe to do so.

slides.title: Deadlock Avoidance
slides.body: Prevention vs Avoidance
tables: Checks each request at run time

slides.title: Why Look Beyond Prevention?
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Prevention is like keeping a door permanently locked so no one can ever get stuck inside — safe, but nobody can use the room. Avoidance is like a guard who opens the door whenever it's safe and only stops you when going in would actually trap someone.

slides.title: Deadlock Avoidance
slides.body:
Maintaining a Safe State
Avoidance assumes every process declares its maximum possible resource need in advance

slides.title: How Deadlock Avoidance Works
slides.body:
Grant : What Keeps System Safe
OS tracks current allocation and future maximum claims
Before granting a request, OS simulates the allocation
Request granted only if system stays in a safe state
Otherwise, the request is delayed
No necessary condition is completely denied
slides.notes: Now, instead of permanently restricting resource requests, deadlock avoidance evaluates each request as it arrives. The operating system keeps track of the resources already allocated and the maximum resources each process may need. Before approving a request, it temporarily checks what the system would look like after the allocation. If the system remains in a safe state, the request is granted; otherwise, it's simply delayed. This way, deadlocks are avoided without eliminating any of the necessary conditions.

slides.title: How Deadlock Avoidance Works
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A tour guide lets a new person join only after checking there are enough seats on the bus for everyone already booked plus everyone expected to board later — so no one is ever left stranded.

slides.title: What Is a Safe State?
slides.body:
Safe Sequence Guarantees Completion
A state is safe if some order lets every process finish without deadlock
………
Safe state
Safe sequence: an order <P1, P2, P3, P4,  ..., Pn> of all processes
slides.notes: Next, the key idea in deadlock avoidance is the safe state. A system is considered safe if there exists at least one order in which all the processes can complete without causing a deadlock. This order is called a safe sequence, where each process gets the resources it needs, finishes its execution, and releases its resources for the remaining processes. As long as such a sequence exists, the system is said to be in a safe state.

slides.title: Safe Sequence
slides.body:
Order of Completion
Each process's remaining need must fit available plus earlier holdings
A satisfied process finishes and releases its resources
Freed resources then unlock the next process in line
At least one such sequence must exist for the state to be safe
………
slides.notes: Now, let's understand how a safe sequence is formed. Starting with the currently available resources, we check whether a process can complete with what is available. Once that process finishes, it releases its resources, increasing the available resources for the next process. This continues until all processes complete. If at least one such order exists, the system is considered to be in a safe state.

slides.title: Safe State
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A chef checks if ingredients are enough to complete every planned dish, one after another, before starting to cook.

slides.title: Checking Safety With Numbers
slides.body: One Resource Type, Three Processes

slides.title: Checking Safety With Numbers
slides.body:
One Resource Type, Three Processes
Total 10 units exist; 7 are already allocated, leaving 3 available units
Available = 3 units at the start
P2 needs only 2 units, so run it first
P2 finishes, releases 2 units, available becomes 5
P1 needs 4 units, available covers it, run P1 next
The safe sequence:
slides.notes: Let's make this concrete with a simple example. Here, there are 10 resource units in total, with 3 currently available. Since P2 needs only 2 units, it can complete first and release its resources, increasing the available units to 5. That is now enough for P1 to finish, and once it releases its resources, P3 can also complete. This gives us the safe sequence P2 → P1 → P3, confirming that the system is in a safe state.

slides.title: Safe State vs Unsafe State
slides.body:
Unsafe Is Risky, Not Always Fatal
Every deadlocked state is unsafe
Not every unsafe state ends in deadlock
Avoidance algorithm never lets the system enter an unsafe state
slides.notes: The key point to remember is that every deadlocked state is unsafe, but an unsafe state does not always lead to a deadlock, which is why avoidance algorithms stop the system from entering an unsafe state in the first place.

slides.title: Safe State vs Unsafe State
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A safe state is like driving with plenty of fuel — you'll surely reach the pump. An unsafe state is like the fuel light being on — you might still make it, but you can't be sure, so a careful driver never lets it get that low.

slides.title: Extending the Resource-Allocation Graph
slides.body:
New Edge for Future Requests
The Resource-Allocation Graph algorithm adapts avoidance to systems with single-instance resources only
slides.notes: Moving on, the idea of deadlock avoidance can also be applied using a Resource Allocation Graph, but this version works only when each resource type has a single instance. To make avoidance possible, the graph is extended so it can represent future resource requests, allowing the operating system to decide whether granting a request would still keep the system safe.

slides.notes: Now, let's look at the claim edge, which is the key addition to the Resource Allocation Graph for deadlock avoidance. A dashed claim edge indicates that a process may request a resource in the future. When the process actually makes that request, the claim edge becomes a request edge, and once the resource is allocated, it changes into an assignment edge. This approach is effective only when each resource type has a single instance.

slides.title: How the Algorithm Decides
slides.body:
Cycle Test
Pi requests Rj: claim edge turns into request edge
OS hypothetically converts request edge into assignment edge
If this creates a cycle, request is denied
Pi must wait, request edge stays as is
If no cycle forms, request is granted safely
slides.notes: Next, let's see how the operating system decides whether a resource request is safe. When a process requests a resource, the operating system temporarily assumes the request has been granted and checks the updated Resource Allocation Graph. If this hypothetical allocation creates a cycle, the request is denied and the process must wait. If no cycle is formed, the request is granted because the system can still operate safely.

slides.title: Cycle Test
slides.body:
Grant Or Wait
Grant
If converting the request edge to an assignment edge forms no cycle, the resource is given immediately
Wait
If it would form a cycle, the request is refused for now and the process waits until it's safe
A cycle in this single-instance graph indicates an unsafe state where deadlock may occur
Claim edges are treated as potential requests, so they are included when checking for a cycle
slides.notes:
Finally, the decision is based on a simple cycle test. 
The operating system temporarily checks what would happen if the requested resource were allocated. 
If the updated graph does not form a cycle, the request is granted immediately. However, 
if granting the resource creates a cycle, the request is postponed and the process must wait 
until the allocation can be made safely. Since claim edges represent possible future requests,
 they are also considered during this cycle check.

slides.title: Cycle Detection Test in RAG
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Finally, think of a narrow one-lane bridge. A car is allowed onto the bridge only if it can cross safely. If allowing it would leave two cars facing each other with neither able to move, the gatekeeper makes it wait. Similarly, the operating system grants a resource request only if it does not create a cycle, preventing a deadlock from forming.

slides.title: Generalising Avoidance for Multiple Instances
slides.body:
Beyond the Single-Instance Graph
The Resource-Allocation Graph algorithm fails once a resource type has multiple instances
Real systems have many instances per resource type
Dijkstra's Banker's Algorithm generalises avoidance using numbers
Named after a banker who never over-lends cash
Checks each request against declared maximum future needs
slides.notes: Moving on, the Resource Allocation Graph approach works only when each resource type has a single instance. Since real systems usually have multiple instances, a different approach is needed. Dijkstra's Banker's Algorithm uses numerical information to check each resource request against the maximum future needs of a process and grants it only if the system remains safe.

slides.title: Banker's Algorithm
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Finally, think of Banker's Algorithm like a bank manager approving loans. Before sanctioning a new loan, the manager checks whether the bank will still have enough money to meet every customer's maximum possible future withdrawal. Similarly, the operating system grants a resource request only if it can still satisfy the maximum future resource needs of all processes

Safety Algorithm

slides.title: Safety Algorithm
slides.body:
Steps
Set Work = Available, Finish[i] = false for all i
Find a process i with Finish[i] false and Need[i] <= Work
If found, Work += Allocation[i], Finish[i] = true, repeat for remaining Process 
If no such process exists, check if all Finish[i] are true
All true means state is safe; otherwise state is unsafe
slides.notes: Now, let's see how the Safety Algorithm checks whether the system is in a safe state. It starts with the currently available resources and looks for a process whose remaining resource need can be satisfied. Once that process finishes, it releases its allocated resources, making them available for others. This continues until either all processes complete, indicating a safe state, or no further process can proceed, which means the state is unsafe.

slides.title: Safety Algorithm
slides.body:
Simulating All Processes Completion
O(m x n^2)
The time complexity of the safety check is
All vector comparisons such as Need[i] <= Work are element-wise: they must hold for every resource type at once
slides.notes: Next, the Safety Algorithm works by simulating the completion of all processes without actually allocating resources. At each step, it checks whether a process's remaining need can be satisfied using the currently available resources. Remember that this comparison is performed for every resource type, and the overall safety check has a time complexity of O(m × n²).

slides.title: Safety Algorithm
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: An exam invigilator checks, in some order, if enough spare answer sheets exist for every remaining student.

slides.title: Resource-Request Algorithm
slides.body:
Steps
Request[i] arrives from process Pi for some resources
Pi
R1
Request[i]
If Request[i] > Need[i], error: exceeds declared maximum claim
If Request[i] > Available, Pi must wait for resources
slides.notes: Now, let's see how the Resource-Request Algorithm begins. When a process Pi submits a Request[i], the operating system first compares Request[i] with Need[i]. If Request[i] is greater than Need[i], the request exceeds the process's declared maximum claim and is treated as an error./ If that check passes, the operating system then compares Request[i] with the Available resources. If enough resources are not available, Pi simply waits until they become available.

slides.title: Resource-Request Algorithm
slides.body:
Deciding to Grant a Request
Pretend to allocate: update Available, Allocation and Need
Run the safety algorithm on this pretended state
Safe: grant permanently; unsafe: rollback and Pi waits
slides.notes: Next, if Request[i] passes the initial checks, the operating system temporarily allocates the requested resources. This means Available is reduced by Request[i], Allocation[i] is increased, and Need[i] is reduced accordingly. The Safety Algorithm is then executed on this temporary state. If the system remains safe, the allocation is made permanent; otherwise, the changes are rolled back, and Pi must wait until the request can be granted safely.

slides.title: Resource-Request Algorithm
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A municipal water office releases extra water only after simulating that every locality's sanctioned share still stays fulfillable.

slides.title: Banker’s Algorithm
slides.body:
Limitations
Each process must declare its maximum need in advance — usually unknown before it runs
The number of processes is fixed — no new process may arrive while it runs
Banker’s Algorithm guarantees safety, but only under strict assumptions that real systems rarely satisfy.
1
2
slides.notes: Finally, while the Banker's Algorithm guarantees that the system stays in a safe state, it relies on some strict assumptions. First, every process must declare its maximum resource requirement before execution, which is often difficult to know in advance. Second, it assumes the number of processes remains fixed, meaning no new process can enter the system while the algorithm is running. These assumptions make the algorithm less practical in many real-world operating systems.

slides.title: Banker’s Algorithm
slides.body:
The number of resource instances is fixed — no resource may fail or be hot-added
Every process must release its resources within a finite time
Banker’s Algorithm guarantees safety, but only under strict assumptions that real systems rarely satisfy.
4
3
Limitations
slides.notes: In addition, the algorithm assumes that the number of resource instances remains fixed, so resources cannot be added or lost while the system is running. It also expects every process to eventually release its resources within a finite time. If these assumptions are violated, the Banker's Algorithm can no longer guarantee that the system will remain safe.

slides.title: Banker’s Algorithm
slides.body:
Conservative by design — it can delay a request that would not actually have deadlocked, lowering utilization
Costly — the O(m x n^2) safety check runs on every request
Banker’s Algorithm guarantees safety, but only under strict assumptions that real systems rarely satisfy.
6
5
Limitations
slides.notes: inally, the Banker's Algorithm is intentionally conservative. It may delay a resource request even when granting it would not actually cause a deadlock, which can reduce overall resource utilization. In addition, every resource request requires running the Safety Algorithm, with a time complexity of O(m × n²), making the approach computationally expensive for large systems.

slides.title: Banker’s Algorithm
slides.body: Assumptions
slides.notes: To summarize, this table explains why the assumptions of the Banker's Algorithm are difficult to satisfy in real systems. Programs rarely know their maximum resource requirement in advance, processes are created and terminated dynamically, resource availability can change as devices are added or fail, and some processes may hold resources for an unpredictable amount of time. Because these assumptions rarely hold together, the Banker's Algorithm is used more as a theoretical approach than in modern operating systems.
tables: Programs seldom know peak demand upfront
Modern systems create and kill processes constantly
Devices can fail or be added at run time
A long or buggy process may hold resources indefinitely

slides.title: A Worked Banker's Algorithm Example
slides.body:
Five Processes, Three Resource Types
Available = (3, 3, 2), the instances still unallocated
Resource types A, B, C have 10, 5 and 7 total instances respectively
slides.notes: At the start, the Available vector is (3, 3, 2), representing the resources that are still free. Using this information, we'll determine whether the system is currently in a safe state.

slides.title: Tracing the Safety Check
slides.body: Finding Step by Step Safe Sequence

slides.title: Tracing the Safety Check
slides.body:
Work starts equal to Available (3,3,2)
Each chosen process adds its Allocation back to Work
All five processes get marked Finish = true
Safe sequence found: P1, P3, P4, P0, P2
Finding Step by Step Safe Sequence
slides.notes: Next, let's trace how the Safety Algorithm works on this example. We begin with Work = Available = (3, 3, 2) and look for a process whose Need can be satisfied. Each time a process completes, it releases its Allocation, which is added back to Work, making more resources available for the remaining processes. Following this approach, all five processes eventually finish, giving the safe sequence P1 → P3 → P4 → P0 → P2. Since every process reaches Finish = true, the system is in a safe state.

slides.title: Resource-Request Walkthrough
slides.body:
Can P1's Request Be Granted?
P1 now requests (1, 0, 2) more units of A, B, C respectively
Check Request <= Need[P1] = (1,2,2): passes
Check Request <= Available = (3,3,2): passes
slides.notes: Now, let's see how the Resource-Request Algorithm works using the same example. Suppose P1 requests Request[P1] = (1, 0, 2). The operating system first checks whether Request[P1] ≤ Need[P1], which it does. It then verifies that Request[P1] ≤ Available, and this condition is also satisfied. Since both initial checks pass, the operating system can move on to the final safety check before deciding whether to grant the request.

slides.title: Can P1's Request Be Granted?
slides.body: Resource-Request Walkthrough
slides.notes: Next, the operating system temporarily allocates the requested resources to P1. As a result, Available becomes (2, 3, 0), Allocation[P1] is updated by adding (1, 0, 2), and Need[P1] becomes (0, 2, 0). The Safety Algorithm is then run on this updated state. Since the system is still safe, the temporary allocation is confirmed, and P1's request is granted permanently.

slides.title: A Request That Is Denied
slides.body:
Granting Leads To An Unsafe State
Continuing from the state right after P1’s request was granted (Available = (2, 3, 0)), suppose P0 now requests (0, 2, 0)
Check Request <= Need[P0] = (7,4,3): passes
Check Request <= Available = (2,3,0): passes
slides.notes: Now, let's look at a case where a request is not granted. After P1's request has been approved, suppose P0 submits Request[P0] = (0, 2, 0). The operating system first checks whether Request[P0] ≤ Need[P0], which passes. It then verifies that Request[P0] ≤ Available, and this condition also passes. Since both checks succeed, the system proceeds to the final Safety Algorithm to determine whether granting the request would still keep the system in a safe state.
